info.name: Traffic Management System
info.description:
Complete API test collection for the Traffic Management System.

Architecture:
- Crow C++ backend   http://localhost:8080  (JSON REST API)
- Django gateway     http://localhost:8000  (HTML web UI, proxies to Crow)
- PostgreSQL         localhost:5432

Import the companion environment file first:
  Traffic_Management_Environment.json

Seeded test data:
  Plates:     AB12CDE (CAR), XY99ZZZ (TRUCK), LM34NOP (MOTORCYCLE), QR56STU (CAR), VW78XYZ (BUS)
  Junctions:  1 = City Centre (50), 2 = North Gate (60), 3 = East Bridge (70), 4 = West Market (50), 5 = South Terminal (60)
  Owner email: alex.carter@example.com (Alex Carter / AB12CDE)

Tip: Run the Crow requests in order within each folder to follow a logical workflow.

item.name: Car Lifecycle (demo)
item.description:
A simple, presentation-friendly walkthrough of one car moving through the system:
1) register a car
2) confirm it exists
3) log a normal drive
4) log a speeding event
5) detect a violation + create a fine
6) pay the fine

Tip: This folder is designed to be run top-to-bottom. It sets a few environment variables automatically (lifecycle_plate, lifecycle_vehicle_id, lifecycle_violation_id, lifecycle_fine_id).

request.description:
Creates one demo car that we will use for the full lifecycle.
If you get 409 (already exists), change new_plate in the environment (e.g. ZZ99NEW → ZZ99AAB) and run again.
Reads all cars so you can quickly point out that the demo car is now stored in the system.

Reads one car by its plate.
Runs best after request 1, which sets lifecycle_plate.
Logs a normal drive event for the demo car. This should not create a fine by itself.

Logs a drive event with a speed above the junction limit.
Even if event_type is PASSAGE, the backend can automatically mark it as SPEEDING when speed_kmh is above the limit.

Turns unprocessed events into a violation and a fine (ticket).
After this request, lifecycle_violation_id and lifecycle_fine_id are set automatically when a result matches the demo plate.

exec: const match = results.find(r => (r.number_plate || r.numberPlate) === plate) || results[0];

request.description:
Reads the fine created for the demo car.
Runs best after request 6, which sets lifecycle_fine_id.
Marks the demo fine as PAID (this is the lifecycle update step).
Confirms the final result after paying: the fine status should be PAID.

item.name: Emergency Lifecycle (demo)
item.description:
A simple walkthrough of the emergency feature:
1) list emergency vehicles
2) create an emergency event (start → target)
3) fetch the event route
4) list affected drivers (emails)

Note: actual email sending is done by the Django web UI (Emergency Control page). This folder focuses on the backend lifecycle and the recipient list.

request.description: Shows which emergency vehicles exist in the system.
Creates an emergency event and returns a computed route from start to target.
Loads the emergency event details including route and estimated time.
Returns the list of drivers whose typical routes overlap with the emergency route (opt-in only).

item.name: Crow API (backend)
item.description: Direct requests to the C++ Crow backend on port 8080. All responses are JSON.

item.name: Vehicles
item.description: Register, list, and inspect vehicles and their owners.

request.description:
Returns all registered vehicles with owner details.
Response: { count, vehicles: [ { id, number_plate, vehicle_type, is_active, created_at, owner: { id, full_name, email, phone } } ] }

Register a new vehicle.
Plate format: 2 uppercase letters + 2 digits + 3 uppercase letters (e.g. ZZ99NEW).
vehicle_type: CAR | TRUCK | MOTORCYCLE | BUS | EMERGENCY
If owner_email already exists the owner record is reused (findOrCreate).
Returns 201 on success, 400 on validation failure, 409 if plate already registered.
Response: { id, number_plate, vehicle_type, owner_id, is_active }
Registers a second vehicle under an existing owner email. The owner record is reused automatically  no duplicate owner is created.

item.name: Junctions & Plate Logs
item.description: Create junctions and manually log plate detection events (simulating ANPR camera input).

request.description:
Returns all junctions with their speed limits.
Response: { count, junctions: [ { id, name, location, speed_limit_kmh, is_active } ] }

Create a new junction/camera point.
Returns 201 with the created junction record.

Log a vehicle passing through a junction. No violation is raised for PASSAGE.
event_type options: PASSAGE | SPEEDING | RED_LIGHT | PARKING
If the plate is not registered, the log is saved as UNREGISTERED with a warning.

Log a speeding event. Include speed_kmh so severity can be calculated against the junction's speed limit.
At junction 1 (limit 50): 92.5 km/h  excess 42.5  CRITICAL severity  fine = 150 - 3.0 = EUR 450.

Log a red-light violation. Always results in CRITICAL severity when violations are detected.
Fine = base_fine (200) - 3.0 = EUR 600.

Log an illegal parking event. Defaults to MEDIUM severity.
Fine = base_fine (80) - 1.5 = EUR 120.
Log a plate that is not in the vehicle registry. Returns status=UNREGISTERED with a warning flag. No fine is issued automatically  the vehicle cannot be linked to an owner.

Returns all plate log entries recorded at a specific junction.
Response: { junction_id, count, logs: [ { id, vehicle_id, number_plate, event_type, status, detected_at, speed_kmh? } ] }

Returns up to 200 most recent plate logs across all junctions (newest first).
Response: { count, logs: [ ... ] }

item.name: Violations & Fines
item.description: Detect violations from plate logs, issue fines, and manage fine payment.

request.description:
Returns up to 100 violations (newest first).
Response: { count, violations: [ { id, vehicle_id, junction_id, violation_type_id, detected_at, severity, evidence_note, status } ] }

Scans unprocessed plate logs at the junction for the past N hours.
Creates a violation + fine for each SPEEDING / RED_LIGHT / PARKING event on a registered vehicle.
Logs are marked processed so they won't be double-charged.
Fine amount = base_fine - severity_multiplier (both stored in violation_types table).
Response: { junction_id, violations_created, results: [ { violation_id, fine_id, number_plate, violation, severity, fine_amount } ] }

Detect violations over the past 24 hours at junction 4 (West Market, limit 50 km/h).
Useful for catching all seeded plate-log events in one call.

Returns a single violation with its linked fine (if any).
Response: { id, vehicle_id, severity, evidence_note, status, fine: { id, amount, status, issued_at } }

item.name: Crow  Issue fine for existing violation

request.description:
Manually issue a fine for a violation that doesn't have one yet.
Returns 409 if a fine already exists for this violation.
Optional body: { "amount": 999.00 } to override the calculated amount.
Response: { fine_id, violation_id, amount, status }

Returns all fines with linked vehicle and owner info.
Response: { count, fines: [ { id, violation_id, amount, status, issued_at, due_date, paid_at, vehicle: { ... }, owner: { ... } } ] }

Returns a single fine record.
Response: { id, violation_id, amount, status, issued_at, due_date, paid_at, vehicle, owner }

item.name: Traffic & Congestion
item.description: Analyse traffic flow, classify congestion levels, predict future congestion, and fetch alternative routes.

request.description:
Counts plate_logs at the junction within the past N hours and classifies:
  < 10 vehicles   LOW
  1019           MODERATE
  2029           HIGH
  30+             SEVERE
Saves a congestion_record to the DB.
HIGH/SEVERE results trigger congestion alert emails (via Django gateway; not from this endpoint directly).
window_hours: 124
Response: { record_id, junction_id, vehicle_count, congestion_level, window_start, window_end }

Scan the full past 24 hours at junction 1. With seed data this should return HIGH or SEVERE.
Note: if testing email dispatch, use the Django congestion page instead  email dispatch runs in the Django gateway layer.

Returns up to 200 stored congestion analysis records (newest first).
Response: { count, records: [ { id, junction_id, time_window_start, time_window_end, vehicle_count, congestion_level, recorded_at } ] }

Returns all congestion records grouped by junction  used by the flow chart on the Django web UI as a time-series view.
Response: { junctions: [ { junction_id, data: [ { time, count, level } ] } ] }

Estimates the next expected congestion level using a 3-sample moving average of the most recent windows for this junction.
Response: { junction_id, predicted_count, predicted_level, method, recommend_diversion }
Junction 4 (West Market) has SEVERE seeded history. Prediction should return HIGH or SEVERE with recommend_diversion: true.
Junction 4 has the most severe congestion history. Use this to see diversion routes from the worst junction.

Returns the full road network graph: every junction (with current congestion level) and every road segment connecting them. Useful for rendering the map or debugging route/tour results.
Response: { junctions: [ { id, name, location, speed_limit_kmh, latitude, longitude, congestion_level } ], roads: [ { id, from_junction_id, to_junction_id, name, distance_km, speed_limit_kmh } ] }

item.name: Django Gateway (web UI)
item.description:
Django serves HTML pages at port 8000. Each page proxies domain data from Crow and renders it as a browser UI.

NOTE: These endpoints return HTML, not JSON. In Postman you will see raw HTML in the response body  that is expected. The primary purpose of including these here is:
  1. Smoke-test that every page loads without a 500 error.
  2. Test the POST form actions (violations detect, congestion analyze, fine pay/cancel) which trigger Django-side logic including email dispatch.

For POST requests: body is application/x-www-form-urlencoded (HTML form encoding), not JSON.

request.description:
Dashboard page. Shows totals for vehicles, violations, pending fines, congestion-prone junctions, and recent fines.
Expect 200 with HTML body.
Lists all registered vehicles. Add ?q=PLATE to filter by plate substring.
Filter vehicle list by plate substring (case-insensitive prefix match).
Shows vehicle info, linked violations, and a form to log the plate at any junction.

Submits the vehicle registration form via Django. Django forwards the JSON payload to Crow (POST /api/vehicles) and redirects to the vehicle list on success.
Expect 302 redirect on success; 200 with error HTML on validation failure.
Note: Django's CSRF middleware may block this from Postman  disable CSRF checking or add a CSRF token if you get 403.
Shows all plate log entries across all junctions.
Filter plate logs by a specific junction.
Shows all violations plus violation type catalogue and a form to trigger violation detection at a junction.

Triggers violation detection through Django. Django calls Crow, then for each fine issued Django sends a fine notification email to the vehicle owner.
Alex Carter (AB12CDE) -> alex.carter@example.com
In development the email prints to the Django container log (console backend). Switch EMAIL_BACKEND to SMTP to deliver real emails.
Expect 200 (re-renders violations page with success message).
Lists all fines with Pay and Cancel buttons.

Pay a fine through the Django gateway. Django calls Crow to update the status and optionally sends a payment-confirmation email.
Expect 200 with updated fines page.

Cancel a PENDING fine through Django.
Expect 200 with updated fines page.

Traffic flow analysis page with two Chart.js visualisations:
  1. Average traffic by hour of day (023)  shows rush-hour patterns
  2. Historical congestion records time-series
Data comes from /api/traffic/flow and /api/traffic/flow/hourly.
Shows congestion-prone junctions, per-junction predictions, and a form to run a fresh analysis.

Runs a congestion analysis at junction 1 over 24 hours via Django.
If the result is HIGH or SEVERE, Django fetches alternative routes from Crow and sends congestion alert emails (with diversion suggestions) to all vehicle owners recently detected at that junction.
With the seed data, junction 1 over 24 hours should produce HIGH/SEVERE  emails dispatched.
Emails print to Django container logs in development mode.

item.name: End-to-End Workflow
item.description: Run these requests in order to exercise the full system from registration through fine payment and congestion alerting.

request.description: Step 1: Register a fresh vehicle. Note the returned id.
Step 2: Log a speeding event at junction 1 (limit 50 km/h). Excess = 35 km/h  CRITICAL severity.

Step 3: Trigger detection through Django so the fine notification email fires. Check the Django container logs to see the email (console backend):
  docker compose logs django
Step 4: Confirm the fine for EE11END appears in the fines list.

item.name: E2E 5  Analyse congestion + trigger alert emails

request.description:
Step 5: Run 24-hour congestion analysis at junction 1 through Django. If HIGH/SEVERE, Django sends congestion alert emails with alternative routes to all owners recently at that junction.

Check logs:
  docker compose logs django
Step 6: Confirm the hourly profile is populated after the congestion analyses above.
